name: Dies irae
summary: F–E–F–D: four notes that can bring death into a piece before a word is sung. The medieval Dies irae chant tells of the Day of Judgement. Later composers carry its opening into symphonies and dances, where the old tune can terrify or grin.

name: B–A–C–H
summary: B♭–A–C–B♮ spells Bach in German note names. He writes that signature into the third subject of his unfinished fugue in The Art of Fugue. Later composers take the four notes as a challenge: a name that can be turned upside down, woven into a fugue or carried into new harmony.

name: The Tristan chord
summary: F–B–D♯–G♯ sounds in bar 2 of Wagner’s Tristan und Isolde prelude. The chord promises a resolution that the music keeps postponing. Its four notes came to stand for longing itself, ready for later composers to quote with devotion or a sly smile.

name: The lament bass
summary: The bass falls through a fourth and starts again. In Purcell’s When I am laid in earth, it fills the descent from G to D with every semitone while Dido sings her farewell. Her phrases change; the bass keeps coming back.

name: La Folia

name: Ode to Joy
summary: Beethoven’s tune begins with two repeated notes, climbs by step and comes back down. It carries Schiller’s appeal to human fellowship into the Ninth Symphony’s finale. That plain, singable line has travelled through piano transcriptions and public ceremonies far beyond the concert hall.

name: Frère Jacques
summary: The familiar round enters Mahler’s First Symphony on a solo double bass, in D minor, over the timpani’s tread. Frère Jacques still repeats its little phrases, but now they belong to a funeral procession. The bassoon and cellos join the round.
